item.title: A Performance Engineering Checklist
item.description: Optimization is the process of discovering which constraint is active and changing the program so that a different constraint becomes active. That is why isolated tricks age badly and models age well. A loop can be slow because it performs unnecessary work, waits on one dependency chain, misses in cache, exceeds memory bandwidth, feeds an unpredictable branch, saturates an execution port, or simply never appears in the program’s profile. Each cause suggests a different transformation.

item.title: Probability and Measurement
item.description: Performance measurements vary. Interrupts arrive, addresses change, predictors learn, caches retain history, and the processor changes frequency. Probability is what lets us separate a repeatable effect from this background variation—and what lets randomized algorithms make useful promises without predicting every run. This appendix develops the small part of probability and statistics used throughout the book. It is not a substitute for experimental design, but it should make the assumptions behind an average, an error bar, or a “with high probability” claim visible.

item.title: Preface
item.description: An algorithm does not run on the RAM model. It runs through a compiler, an instruction set, a speculative out-of-order core, several caches, a virtual-memory system, and whatever operating system happened to schedule it. Asymptotic analysis deliberately hides these details; performance engineering begins when the hidden constants become the problem. This book studies the boundary between algorithms and modern hardware. The first part is about one CPU thread: how to measure it, reason about it, and reshape an algorithm so that the core can execute more useful work in parallel.
